title: Disagreeing with love
hookLine: streams disagree on practice, conversion and marriage, and still share one people
last: TZEDAKAH: GIVING THAT SETS THE WORLD RIGHT.

cards: Two schools of teachers, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, disagree. Not once: over and over, on law after law.
In the Talmud's telling, each house insisted the law followed them, and the argument would not end. Then a voice came from heaven and settled it. But listen to how.
The voice did not say one side was right and the other wrong. It said something stranger, and the rabbis kept the sentence.

teach.b: Disagreeing with love. Four turns. First, the voice.

In the Talmud's telling, it said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the House of Hillel. Both views are words of the living God; one still becomes the practice. Second, why Hillel.

teach.h: HILLEL: GENTLE, HUMBLE, OTHER VIEW FIRST.
teach.b: The Talmud asks that itself, and answers: Hillel's students were gentle and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even said Shammai's first. They won the law by the way they held the argument.

teach.h: A DISPUTE FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.
teach.b: The Mishnah says a dispute for the sake of heaven will last, and one that isn't, won't. Its example of the first kind is Hillel and Shammai.
Its example of the second is Korah and his company, who rose against Moses for power. The question isn't whether people argue. It's what the argument is for.
Fourth, the families. The two houses disagreed even about laws of marriage, which could have split them into two peoples.
Yet the Talmud reports they did not refrain from marrying into each other's families.
Today the streams disagree on real things: how to keep Shabbat, how a person converts, whose conversion counts, which marriages a rabbi will perform.

Those disputes can wound, and love doesn't mean pretending they don't matter. The old model offers something narrower and harder: say the other side's view first, say it well, and keep the families at one table.

how: Jewish study is built on recorded disagreement: the Talmud preserves minority views beside the law, and study partners are expected to argue hard while learning each other's reasoning.

o: agreeing to drop a dispute to keep the peace
never saying out loud that you disagree
arguing for the sake of heaven, other view first

games.q: disagreeing with love — tap the pairs.
p: the words of the living God

s: the voice from heaven said the House of Shammai was wrong
it said these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel.
the Talmud says Hillel's students even stated Shammai's view first
they were gentle and humble, and that is why the law follows them.
the two houses stopped marrying into each other's families
the Talmud reports they did not refrain, despite disagreeing on marriage law.

games.q: you're a student in the House of Hillel. you're sure your school is right, and the House of Shammai is in the room. what do you do?
o: state your view loudly and leave.
teach Shammai's view, and say it first, then your own.
refuse to discuss it with them at all.
games.why: the Talmud says Hillel's students taught both views and said Shammai's first, and that this is why the law follows Hillel.

practice: Bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters; not your worst fight, just one you can carry for two minutes.
Do what Hillel's students did: say their view first, silently, in its strongest and fairest form, then say your own just as fairly, and notice whether anything softens.
If you pray, hold that person in your prayer before you let them go.

wordCard.voice: Disagreeing with love. Holding a real dispute for the sake of heaven: stating the other view first and fairly, and staying one family. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: these and these are the words of the living God, Eruvin 13b.

carryVoice: Your line: disagree with love. The other side's view, said first and said well. Until tomorrow.
